analysis.body:
The most detailed public accounting of federal AI deployment in the United States comes from the U.S. Government Accountability Office, which found that twenty of twenty-three major federal agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported having no uses for AI at all. Of those roughly 1,200 cases, only about 200 were in active production at the time of the review, meaning the large majority remained in planning or earlier lifecycle stages. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of use cases. The applications agencies described ranged from analyzing drone photography and camera and radar data for border activity to targeting scientific specimens on planetary rovers and identifying information security threats.

Per GAO, the inventory data itself carries significant reliability problems. Only five of the twenty reporting agencies provided comprehensive information for each of their use cases, while the other fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data, including missing lifecycle stage designations and, in two cases, use cases that agencies later determined were not AI at all. GAO also found that no government-wide guidance exists on how agencies should acquire and use AI, which limits consistent management across the federal enterprise. Ten of twenty-three agencies fully implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed acquisition and use guidance, and the Office of Personnel Management had not established or updated occupational categories for employees performing AI work.

On the funding side, per GAO, the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, representing two of the more complete compliance records among the agencies reviewed.

The broader policy environment is tracked across multiple organizations. Stanford HAI notes in its AI Index that a widening gap has opened between what AI can do and how prepared governments are to manage it, with the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology falling behind rapid capability growth. The OECD.AI Policy Observatory monitors national AI strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, tracking more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives, and emphasizes principles around transparency, fairness, robustness, and safety for trustworthy AI development. Oxford Insights produces a Government AI Readiness Index that scores countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, offering the standard cross-national comparison for where governments stand relative to one another.

For those considering AI deployment in or alongside government, the GAO record suggests that early-mover agencies are concentrating use cases in data analysis, surveillance-adjacent applications, and scientific work, while the compliance and governance scaffolding to support broader deployment remains unfinished. The legislative environment is particularly active, with 2,426 AI bills tracked across 53 jurisdictions in the United States alone according to this site's AI Laws section, updated daily from LegiScan. Anyone deploying AI in a government context should expect the regulatory floor to shift materially in the near term, and should treat the absence of government-wide acquisition guidance not as permission but as a risk factor that agencies themselves have been told to address.
